lesson_title: Tilt a File, Build a Mountain Range
hook_text: The Magaliesberg is a lever-arch file with a book shoved under one end. Seriously.
clip_script: Take a lever-arch file full of paper and lay it flat — that is the Karoo, flat layers, flat-topped hills. Now slide a book under one end so the file tilts. You just built a new kind of mountain. Run your hand down the top cover: a long smooth ramp — the dip slope, riding on the surface of one strong rock layer. Now look at the raised end of the file, where all the page-edges are cut off: a short steep face — the scarp slope, slicing across every layer at once. Dip follows, scarp cuts. Four words, every diagram labelled. Now turn the tilt like a dial. Gentle, up to about 25 degrees: a cuesta — a wheelchair ramp with a cliff at the back. Crank it to between 25 and 45: the ramp gets too steep to cycle, the ridge sharpens — a homoclinal ridge, and you have driven past one, because that is exactly what the Magaliesberg is: a hundred-kilometre quartzite file tilted on its side. Now slam the dial past 45, pages standing almost upright. The ramp vanishes. Both sides steep, narrow spiky crest, like the bristles down a hedgehog's spine — a hogsback. And the punchline: the steeper the layers lean, the narrower and more even the ridge becomes, until you cannot tell its two faces apart. One file, one dial, three mountains.
visual_style: A real lever-arch file tilting in stages and morphing into ridge cross-sections, each dial setting stamping its angle and name on screen, ending on an aerial sweep along the Magaliesberg with the file ghosted underneath.
mood: Hands-on aha moment scaled up to mountain size.
pacing: Quick tactile open, three clean beats as the dial turns, satisfying landing on the real range.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and name every tilted ridge you drive past.
